links.claim: I run procurement for a mid-size fabless shop, and I have spent most of 2026 staring at Kestrel Semiconductor's Penang advanced-packaging queue. Here is the blunt version: the queue has been shrinking, and it has been shrinking faster than anyone on the buy side expected. I have the dated numbers, and I have the week counts, because that is the only way to talk about this business without getting lied to.
links.passage: I run procurement for a mid-size fabless shop, and I have spent most of 2026 staring at Kestrel Semiconductor's Penang advanced-packaging queue. Here is the blunt version: the queue has been shrinking, and it has been shrinking faster than anyone on the buy side expected. I have the dated numbers, and I have the week counts, because that is the only way to talk about this business without getting lied to.

links.claim: On 1 June 2026, Kestrel's Penang advanced-packaging lead time was 26 weeks. That was the number we built our H2 allocation plan around. It was ugly. It meant anything we booked in June landed in December, which meant our Q4 customer commitments were effectively locked before we had a single wafer out of the foundry. We were quoting our own customers at 30 weeks and padding the back end because we did not trust the 26.

links.claim: By 1 August 2026, the same Penang line was quoting 22 weeks. That is a four-week improvement in eight weeks, which sounds modest until you annualise it. Then on 15 September 2026, the number came in at 18 weeks. So from 1 June 2026 to 15 September 2026, we went from 26 weeks to 18 weeks, a cut of 31%, while capacity grew from 11,000 units to 16,000 units a month. That is eight weeks of lead time gone in fifteen weeks of calendar time. I have been doing this for eleven years and I have never seen a packaging queue compress that fast without a demand shock behind it.

links.claim: The obvious explanation is capacity. Kestrel commissioned Phase 2 at Penang on 15 August 2026. That is the date I have from the supplier's own capacity notice, and it lines up with the 1 August 2026 quote of 22 weeks, because the line was already loading Phase 2 tools in late July. Phase 2 is the advanced-packaging expansion, the one they have been teasing since 2024. It is real, it is running, and it is the reason the queue is moving.

links.claim: The less obvious explanation is mix. Kestrel has been quietly pushing lower-layer flip-chip work off Penang and onto its other back-end sites, which frees the Penang line for the high-layer-count stuff that actually pays. I do not have that in writing. I have it from three separate conversations with people who would know, and the behaviour of the quotes supports it. Our simple parts are suddenly quoting out of a different site. Our hard parts are still Penang, but they are quoting shorter.

links.claim: Here is the part that matters for anyone building a dual-source strategy. The Johor alternative, the one everyone has been treating as the safe fallback, was still at 24 weeks on 15 September 2026. Read that again. Penang is at 18 weeks. Johor is at 24 weeks. The fallback is now six weeks slower than the primary.

links.claim: That is a complete inversion of where we were in the spring. Back in Q1, Johor was the fast lane and Penang was the queue you endured because you had no choice. Now the fast lane is Penang and Johor is the queue. If you are still splitting your volume 50/50 on the assumption that Johor is the safer bet, you are paying a six-week penalty for the privilege of being wrong.

links.claim: I am not saying abandon Johor. I am saying reprice it. If your allocation model still treats Johor as the low-risk path, your model is stale. The risk premium has flipped.
links.passage: I am not saying abandon Johor. I am saying reprice it. If your allocation model still treats Johor as the low-risk path, your model is stale. The risk premium has flipped.

links.claim: I moved our Q4 volume. Not all of it, but the majority. We had been running roughly 60/40 Penang/Johor since the spring, and I have pushed that to 80/20 as of the third week of September. The reason is simple arithmetic. At 18 weeks, Penang lands our Q4 build in the first half of January. At 24 weeks, Johor lands it in early March. One of those keeps our customer commitments. The other one does not.

links.claim: The counterargument is concentration risk. If Penang sneezes, we are exposed. That is fair, and I am not pretending it is not. But concentration risk is a probability, and a six-week lead-time gap is a certainty. I will take the certain six weeks and manage the probability with buffer stock on the two parts where a Penang hiccup would actually hurt us.

links.claim: The other thing I am doing is re-quoting everything. Every PO we have out with Kestrel, I have asked for a fresh lead time against the 15 September 2026 number. Some of them came back at 18 weeks. Some came back longer because of specific layer counts or specific substrate constraints. The headline number is not the number for your part. The headline number is the number for the easiest part on the line. Do not plan against the headline.

links.claim: Kestrel is not doing this out of generosity. They are doing it because Phase 2 gave them capacity and because they want the high-layer-count volume, and the way you win high-layer-count volume is by being the fastest quote in the room. The 26 weeks to 18 weeks move is a commercial play as much as a capacity play. That is fine. I do not need my suppliers to be charitable. I need them to be predictable, and right now Penang is more predictable than it has been all year.

links.claim: The question is whether it holds. Phase 2 is commissioned, but commissioning is not the same as mature yield. If the new line runs into a substrate problem in October, that 18 weeks goes back to 22 in a hurry. I have seen it happen. So I am treating the 18 weeks as real but not permanent. I am booking against it. I am not signing annual contracts against it.

links.claim: If you are still quoting your own customers off a 26-week assumption, you are leaving weeks on the table. If you are still routing volume to Johor because it used to be the fast lane, you are paying for a memory. The numbers as of 15 September 2026 are 18 weeks Penang, 24 weeks Johor, and a Phase 2 line that came online on 15 August 2026. That is the whole picture. Act accordingly.
